# Overview

Here I briefly update on my progress on finalizing my multi-variate meta-analytical Distributed Lag Non-linear Model (DLNM). First, I provide a brief overview of relevant descriptive statistics for this report. Second, I will outline my exposure selection and sensitivity analysis, providing an explanation for variable inclusion and model parameters (e.g. seasonality, autocorrelation, cross basis degrees of freedom and model family). Then, I report preliminary outputs for overall and city specific results, followed by seasonal and population group models. Finally, I give my suggestions in moving forward and outstanding questions to the team.

As a reminder, my research questions for this analysis are as follows:

-   **Lag-response: How is the effect of a single exposure at time** $t$ **distributed across future time points (lags)?** *E.g. If it's hot today, does the health impact occur immediately, or does it show up in 2–3 days?*

-   **Exposure-response: How do different levels of the exposure variables affect the outcome?** *E.g. How does the risk of hospital admissions change when temperature increases from 20°C to 30°C?*

-   **Do the exposure–lag effects vary across vulnerable groups?** *E.g. Are children under 5 or the elderly more sensitive to specific temperatures or lag duration compared to the general population?*

-   **Do the exposure–lag effects vary across location?** *E.g. Are some locations more at risk due to their unique geographies (i.e. elevation) or population profiles (i.e. population density)?*

The DLNM models were based on papers by Gasparrini 2015 and fit using tutorials sourced [here](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22807043/). Parameters selection approach was adapted from a supplementary material by Xiao 2017, sourced [here](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0160412016304317?via%3Dihub#s0005).

This section provides an summary of descriptive statistics of outcomes and exposures relevant to the report, rather than a comprehensive overview. This is highlighted in the study overview figure below (@fig-study-area). Please note that Bilaspur is included in the figures below simply to highlight it has a short time series, thus justifying its exclusion at this stage.

## Outcome variables

Our primary outcome of concern is total patient admission across our 8 hospitals of interest (@fig-outcome-loc). These are mostly normally distributed, with Hamirpur having the highest footfall and Reckong Peo having the lowest (remember we are ignoring Bilaspur here). Ward footfall and types of wards varies widely across locations and time, making it difficult to select an inclusive list to analyse (@fig-ward-loc, @fig-ts-ward). However, considering the nature of our weather exposures, we are more interested in unplanned emergency admissions. There is only one location with a high enough daily average footfall and time series that can allow for this type of analysis: Hamirpur (@fig-ts-emg-loc). This is why we focus on this site in SECTION X.

## Data transformations

Rainfall required additional transformation due to its nature and distribution. Daily rainfall effects are often small and have limited observable effects on their own. Following common practice, we chose to model rainfall as a rolling 7-day sum to better capture cumulative effects that are more observable. However, calculating these cumulative effects did not improve the variables extreme inverse exponential distribution and required a transformation to improve model interpretability. Therefor, to offset the zero values, we shifted the variable by 10 and log transformed it. These distributions are summarised in @fig-tp-dist.

![Comparison of rainfall transformation distributions](figures/descriptive/desc_4_tp_dist.png){#fig-tp-dist}

# Exposure selection

## Non-parameter correlation test

Spearman correlation tests indicate that the link between total patients and various atmospheric exposures is small in magnitude (@fig-corrplot). Temperature–particularly mean, max and wet-bulb temperature–have the highest correlation with hospital admissions (0.21), followed by wind speed (-0.19). Links to rainfall, diurnal range, air pollution and relative humidity are tenuous. However, it is possible that associations are obscured by spatial-temporal trends, so I further assessed associations via a XGBoost feature importance model, controlling for such factors.

![Correlation plot of total patient outcome and atmospheric predictors.](figures/sensitivity/SF_corr_plot.png){#fig-corrplot}

## XGBoost feature importance model

Overall (i.e. across all locations), the XGBoost model indicated that spatial-temporal factors like autocorrelation, weekday, time, population density and elevation outweighed the importance of weather exposures (@fig-xgb-all). However, among the weather exposures, temperature–particularly maximum and wet-bulb temperature– ranked most important, followed by wind speed, air pollution, relative humidity and rainfall. These weather effects were very small relative to other model factors and slightly differ from the correlation tests.

It is possible that feature importance differed across locations. To asses this, we ran the XG boost algorithm for each site subset with hyper parameters optimized for each location. We found that feature importance varied considerably across sites (@fig-xgb-loc), with patterns in feature importance difficult to identify. To delve deeper, we counted the frequency at which each feature appeared in the top and bottom half of the feature gain list (@tbl-xgb-loc). Features were considering more "important if the frequency at which they appeared in the top half features was greater than their occurrence in the bottom features".

Autocorrelation and lagged effects are also important to consider. Additional total and city specific XGBoost models were optimized with 14 lags for total patients and all atmospheric variables. The overall models found most patterns to be attributable to outcome time and autocorrelation effects (notably lags 1, 7, 14), with max temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and mean temperature making the top 20 important features (gain effects were \<0.01). No lagged atmospheric variables made the top 20 features. City-specific models reflected similar patterns for outcome time and correlation effects, though atmospheric variables varied more widely with lagged effects only occasionally making the top 20 features. Frequency comparison tables of top 20 feature occurrence (@tbl-xgb-loc-lag) further confirmed this and max temperature, wind speed, diurnal temperature range and mean temperature (no lags) as the most relevant weather exposures.

From these tests, max/mean temperature and wind speed are clearly important factors, but it is difficult to draw more decisive conclusions on other weather exposures. Based on literature and partner input, we also know rainfall is one of the most challenging weather extremes in the area but this is not reflected in our XGBoost models. Considering this, we will focus on maximum temperature, rainfall and wind speed in the following analyses, to minimize model complexity.

![XGBoost feature importance model of atmospheric exposures, controlling for spatial–temporal variables](figures/sensitivity/SF_xgb_importance.png){#fig-xgb-all}

![Location-specific XGBoost feature importance model of atmospheric exposures, controlling for spatial–temporal variables](figures/sensitivity/SF_xgb_importance_loc.png){#fig-xgb-loc}

Based on exposure inclusion tests and partner input, I chose to include the following weather variables in my model:

-   Daily maximum temperature (°C)

-   7-day cumulative precipitation (mm) (with log-shift transformation)

-   Daily average wind speed (km/hr)

**Note**: [All weather exposures in subsequent models use a relative scale according to location. Therefore x-axis are represented as percentiles. All predictions use the 0th percentile as a reference, except temperature which is non-linear and thus uses the 50th percentile.]{style="color:darkred;"}

# Sensitivity analysis

While we were initially interested in pooled effects across sites, our exposure selection models indicate a high degree of variation between hospital sites. It is therefore clear that we need to examine single site models, in addition to pooled effect models, which will require additional sensitivity tests. The following sensitivity analysis was conducted to select DLNM parameters appropriate for the pooled models (i.e. including all 8 site ) and each individual site model.

For each pooled and individual model, decisions are guided by theory and pooled AIC model criteria and pooled ACF plots, where appropriated. A one-way analysis strategy was applied, evaluating one decision at a time while keeping others fixed. Model choices were assessed sequentially, following their relative importance and the logical order of the time-series modelling process, with each step informed by the previous one. Lag and shape parameter tests specifically assessed the impacts of maximum temperature, rainfall and wind speed as predictors of hospital admissions.

**Note**: [To minimise repetitive plots, I will just focus on the pooled results below. I have extract the exact same plots for each individual site model, which I can provide if necessary.]{style="color:darkred;"}

## Controlling for long-term trends and seasonality

Previous studies show that annual hospital admission patterns vary irregularly across locations, making explicit time functions (e.g., month- or year-specific indicators) unsuitable for adjusting long-term trends and seasonality, as they assume constant or repeating temporal patterns. We therefore used a flexible smoothing function of time to account for unmeasured time-varying confounders. In the sensitivity analysis, I varied the df of time splines from 1 to 12 *df* per year and evaluated model fit via AIC scores (@fig-sens-seas). Here, we can see the model fit gradually decreases until the df reaches 10 per year, and then remains stable. However, the difference between *df*'s 8-10 is negligible, so we will **opt for a simpler model fit at *df*=8.**

![Pooled AIC criterion for different degrees of freedom (df) for long-term seasonality trends.](figures/sensitivity/SM_1A_pooled_longterm_AIC.png){#fig-sens-seas fig-align="left"}

## Controlling for autocorrelations related to disease transmission

Hospital admissions encompass many health outcomes, including infectious and non-infectious diseases. Unlike non-infectious diseases, the transmission of infectious diseases may cause strong residual auto correlations, even when seasonal and long-term trends are controlled for.

Autocorrelation plots indicated that there was substantial autocorrelation at weekly intervals. We tested lags from 1-14, where a lag of *k* represents the cumulative effect of lags 1 through *k* (e.g., a lag of 7 includes lags 1–7). These tests indicated that a model with lags 1-14 had the best AIC criteria (@fig-sens-auto), but this did not eliminate autocorrelation from the model (@fig-sens-auto-acf).

Initially, I tested lags from 1-30, which indicated lags 1-29 as the most appropriate lags and this reduced autocorrelation a bit more. This range, however, goes beyond normal autocorrelation and flags other underlying issues with the model that must be further explored. When examining the city specific parameter tests, it seems that there autocorrelation varies widely across sites.

![Pooled AIC criterion for different patient lags to account for autocorrelation trends.](figures/sensitivity/SM_2A_pooled_autocorr_AIC.png){#fig-sens-auto}

![Comparison of ACF plots for models with no lag and model with the lowest AIC score (i.e. lags 1-29).](figures/sensitivity/SM_2A_pooled_autocorr_ACF.png){#fig-sens-auto-acf}

## Choices of the flexibility of the lag of the exposure-response relationships

Identifying the appropriate range of exposure-response lags is key to obtaining accurate estimations. Since hospital admissions address a multitude of infectious and non-infectious diseases -- each with different long- and short-term transmission routes that are variably influenced by meteorological factors -- it will not be possible for us to specifically control for all possible lag periods. Considering this, we chose to examine a set period between 0 to 14 days, because we are primarily interested in short-term, acute weather-induced health effects. This was fit as an unconstrained distribute lag model with a *df* of 4, which is widely applied across DLNM studies.

We found that the lag basis for maximum temperature, rainfall and wind speed performed best with lag *df*'s of 6, 5 and 3 respectively. Since rainfall AIC scores for *df*=3 was similar to 5, we selected to more parsimonious parameter. Therefore, we used ***df*****'s of 6, 3 and 3 for maximum temperature, rainfall and wind speed**, respectively.

![Pooled AIC criterion for different degrees of freedom (df) for lags of individual weather exposures.](figures/sensitivity/SM_3A_pooled_arglag_AIC.png){#fig-sens-arglag}

## Choices of the flexibility of the shape of the exposure-response relationships

With the lag structure identified, we then assessed the shape of each exposure-response relationship and appropriate flexibility. Prior research thus suggests that the relationships between my weather phenomena and hospital admissions are non-linear. That said, with the exception of temperature and relative humidity, most studies of meteorological variables opt for a simple form of representation and assume a linear relationship with few lags. Therefore, we tested linear and non-linear relationship for all predictors. Non-linear models were described by natural cubic splines with *df*'s varied from 3 to 8. the figure below summarizes AIC results across weather variables.

We found that the exposure basis for both maximum temperature and wind speed performed best with natural splines with *df*'s of 3, whereas rainfall preferred a linear fit (@fig-sens-argvar). However, after cross comparing the AIC scores with variable exposure distributions (@fig-sens-argvar-dis), it seems that a natural spline with *df*=4 may be more appropriate for rainfall, since the relationship generally remained stable after this *df*, which is in agreement with previous studies. Therefore, we used natural splines with ***df*****'s of 3, 4 and 3 for maximum temperature, rainfall and wind speed**, respectively.

![Pooled AIC criterion for different degrees of freedom (df) for exposure-response shape of individual weather exposures.](figures/sensitivity/SM_4A_pooled_argvar_AIC.png){#fig-sens-argvar}

![Comparison of maximum temperature (red), rainfall (blue) and windspeed (purple) exposure-response shape across degrees of freedom.](figures/sensitivity/SM_4A_pooled_argvar_DIS.png){#fig-sens-argvar-dis}

## Choices of the statistical models

Up until this point, all tests have been conducted with quasi-Poisson models for the sake of parsimony. However, both the quasi-Poisson and negative binomial models are commonly used in healthcare modelling to address over dispersion issues. However, each model assumes a different relationship of variance to the mean. While both account for additional noise in the data, the quasi-Poisson assumes a constant multiplier, whereas the negative binomial allows the multiplier to vary across groups (Ver Hoef JM, Boveng PL 2007). We assessed how each model effected the shape of the temperature and total hospital admission relationship (@fig-sens-shape). There was a notable difference in precipitation estimates, so we chose the negative binomial model for our final model.

To summarise, we selected to following parameters for our pooled results:

-   Longterm=8; Autocorrelation=14; mx2t_arglag=6; tp_arglag =5; fg10_arglag=3; mx2t_argvar=3; tp_argvar=1; fg10_argvar=3; shape=binom.

![Comparison of overall distribution for quasi poisson and negative binomial models, both fit with identical parameters.](figures/sensitivity/SM_5A_pooled_shape.png){#fig-sens-shape}

# Preliminary results

## Analysis 1: Overall

This analysis includes data for 8 hospitals across Himachal Pradesh between 2015 and 2020. Please note that rainfall is log transformed for modelling, which is why the city specific estimates look pushed to oneside in plots. All exposures were modelled on a relative scale which greatly improved model interpretability. Location specific percentile look ups can be found with the **supplementary tables** attached with this report. These results are summarized as follows:

-   **Overall** (@fig-res1-overall): Looking at cumulative effects across lags, the only weather exposure to have a significant effect on admissions is maximum temperature. Lower temperature percentiles is linked with notable decreases in hospital admissions.

-   **Lag-response** (@fig-res1-lr): The lag-response plots suggest that cold temperatures elicit an significant decrease in admissions the day of exposure, but an increase in relative risk of admission at lag 3. Warm temperatures have no effect across lags. Higher precipitation percentiles are only notable at lags 4-5. Wind has no effect across lags.

-   **Exposure-response** (@fig-res1-er): These lag relationships are similarly reflected in the exposure-response plots. For instance, we observe a \~30% decrease in relative risk of hospital admissions the day of occurrence when cold temepratures fall below the 20th percentile. An additional plot is required to illustrate the 4% increase in admissions at Lag 3 – which is marginally observed at lags 14 as well. On the day of occurrence, a 3% decrease in admissions is observed when precipitation exceeds the 80th percentile. A small but significant increase in admissions is observed 5 days after precipitation exceeds the 90th percentile. No effects are observed for wind.

![Cumulative relative risk (RR) of exposure-response for total hospital admissions across all time for each weather predictors. Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/MF_1A_total_er_overall.png){#fig-res1-overall}

![Relative risk (RR) of weather lag-response for total hospital admissions, by percentile (10th, 25th, 27th and 90th). Red corresponds to daily average maximum temperature (mx2t), blue corresponds to 7-day cumulative precipitation (tp), purple corresponds to daily maximum wind speed (fg10). Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/MF_1B_total_lr.png){#fig-res1-lr}

![Relative risk (RR) of weather exposure-response for total hospital admissions, by lag (0, 5, 10 and 14 days). Red corresponds to daily average maximum temperature (mx2t), blue corresponds to 7-day cumulative precipitation (tp), purple corresponds to daily maximum wind speed (fg10). Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, and rainfall uses the 20th percentile.](figures/MF_1C_total_er.png){#fig-res1-er}

### City-specific differences

Using the same model fit as above, we can examine the city specific differences, plotted against the pooled results. The plots below provide the cumulative exposure-response effects over time for each weather exposure. BLUP estimates are city-specific coefficients weighted by the pooled effects. **Please note that city plots are presented from lowest elevation (top left) to highest elevation (bottom right).** Here we find:

-   **Maximum temperature** (@fig-res1-temp): Una seems to be particularly susceptible to cold temperatures below the 20% percentile, but confidence intervals are too wide and thus insignificant. The only other city with a notable cold temperature effect is Chamba, where we observe a 20% decrease in admissions when maximum temperatures dip below the 20th percentile. Regarding warm temperatures, Dharamshala has a 30% increase in admissions when temperatures exceed the 80th percentile. Kullu also exhibits an increase relative to warm temperatures, but the link is marginally insignificant. No other effects are observed, but it is worth noting that low laying sites (top row) seem more effected by cold and high altitude sites (bottom row) seem more effected by heat.

-   **Precipitation** (@fig-res1-tp): Only Dharamshala shows a steep increase in admissions due to precipitation (up to \~20%), but this is only marginally significant. There are no other observable effects for other locations, but trends suggest that higher altitude sites may be more effected by precipitation.

-   **Wind speed** (@fig-res1-fg10): The effects we see for wind speed are largely insignificant. However, Hamirpur appears to have incredibly high relative risks of admissions due to wind speed (500% increase). This is a questionable output perhaps linked to parameters fit, which requires further investigation.

![Daily maximum temperature exposure-response, by city. The 50th percentile is used as reference.](figures/MF_1D_city_tmp_er.png){#fig-res1-temp}

![7-day cumulative precipitation exposure-response, by city. The 0th percentile as reference.](figures/MF_1E_city_tp_er.png){#fig-res1-tp}

### Case study: Chamba & Dharamshala

Considering the findings above, it is worth examining a specific city to understand how these cumulative exposures vary across lags. Here we use Chamba and Dharmashala as case studies to understand how their respective exposure-response relationships vary across lags.

-   **Chamba** (@fig-res1-chamb): When temperatures dip below the 20th percentile, the relative risk of hospital admissions decreases by over 10% on the day of occurrence. Precipitation decreases admissions by over \~7% on the day of occurrence, but increases admissions at lag 10. No other effects were observed at other lags or for other weather variables. Wind speed had no effect.

-   **Dharamshala** (@fig-res1-daram): Similar cold temperature effects were observed for Dharamshala, but warm weather also has an influence on admissions from the day of occurrence until lag 10. While marginally insignificant, precipitation is linked to a 4% increase in admissions when the 80th percentile is reached. Wind speed had no effect.

![Chamba exposure-response relationship, by weather percentiles, from pooled model. Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/SF_1H_cham_er.png){#fig-res1-cham}

![Dharamshala exposure-response relationship, by weather percentiles, from pooled model. Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/SF_1J_dharam_er.png){#fig-res1-daram}

## Analysis 2: City-specific models

Now that we have examined the outputs from the pooled model, let's briefly cross compare outputs for the city specific models, again using Chamba and Dharamsala as case studies. The results and parameters selected for these sites are as follows:

-   **Chamba** (@fig-res2-chamb): Despite slightly different parameters, trends from the city-specific model are quite similar to those from the pooled effect, especially for temerpature. Rainfall is slightly different, with a reverse trends for lag 5 and no effect for lag 14. Wind speed trends are more clear and do not over fit the data.

    -   [*Parameters*]{.underline}*: Longterm=7; Autocorrelation=13; mx2t_arglag=4; tp_arglag =6; fg10_arglag=4; mx2t_argvar=3; tp_argvar=1; fg10_argvar=1; shape=binom.*

-   **Dharamshala** (@fig-res2-dharam): Dharamshala trends are similarly stable in the stand alone model, though it seems to be over fitting the data somewhat. The rainfall patterns are very different and show strong signs of of over fitting, ultimately resulting in insignificant results across lags.

    -   [*Parameters*]{.underline}*: Longterm=8; Autocorrelation=13; mx2t_arglag=6; tp_arglag =5; fg10_arglag=5; mx2t_argvar=5; tp_argvar=4; fg10_argvar=3; shape=binom.*

My first take away from this is that the stand alone models parameters need further tuning to remove the over fitting observed. However, this comparison also suggests that the stand alone model's with city-specific parameters may improve estimates but the outputs are relatively comparable from these 2 examples.

![Chamba exposure-response relationship, by weather percentiles, from stand alone model. Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/SF_2B_spec_cham_er.png){#fig-res2-chamb}

![Dharamshala exposure-response relationship, by weather percentiles, from stand alone model. Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/SF_2A_spec_dharam_er.png){#fig-res2-dharam}

## Analysis 3: Seasonal differences

After conducting the initial primary analysis provided above, it was noted that these relationships likely differ by season. To assess this, I ran two additional models, which were separated into winter/pre-monsoon months (January-May) and Monsoon/Post-monsoon months (June-December). Model parameters remained the same as above. Our results are as follows:

Winter months are more sensitive to heat and rainfall, whereas summer months do not show any notable effects, when examining overall trends (@fig-res3-seas). When examined by specific lags (@fig-res3-seas-er), these winter effects remain but summer months exhibit more sensitive to cold weather, particularly at lags 0 and 14. This suggests that unseasonal weather may have a greater impact on hospital admissions.

![Relative risk (RR) of weather exposure-response for total hospital admissions during winter, by lag (0, 5, 10 and 14 days). Red corresponds to daily average maximum temperature (mx2t), blue corresponds to 7-day cumulative precipitation (tp), purple corresponds to daily maximum wind speed (fg10). Temperature uses the 50th percentile as reference, all other exposures use the 0th percentile.](figures/MF_3A_seas_overall.png){#fig-res3-seas}

![Relative risk (RR) of weather exposure-response for total hospital admissions during summer, by lag (0, 5, 10 and 14 days). Red corresponds to daily average wet-bulb temperature (wb), blue corresponds to daily total rainfall (tp), green corresponds to daily relative humidity (rh).](figures/MF_3C_seas_er.png){#fig-res3-seas-er}

## Analysis 4: Population differences

Finally, we ran population specific models to understand gender and age differences. Here I present results for specific outcomes based on significant lags identified in the overall model. Model parameters remained the same as previous analyses.

Across variables, the relationship between exposures and admissions remains stable. However the magnitude and significance of the relationship varies across populations. For maximum temperatures (@fig-res4-temp), women, children under 5, aged 5-14 and over 65 are more affected by cold weather the day of exposure than other population groups. There is no observable effect for precipitation wind speed (@fig-res4-tp, @fig-res4-fg10), though increased wind speeds are significantly correlated to an increase in children under 5 admissions, but only up until the 70th percentile.

This suggests that weather exposures have a variable effect across populations, but additional statistical tests wouldbe required to test significance of the difference between groups.

![Maximum temperature exposure-response relationship (Lag 0), disaggregated by population groups](figures/MF_4_disag_er0_tmp.png){#fig-res4-temp}

![Precipitation exposure-response relationship (Lag 10), disaggregated by population groups](figures/MF_4_disag_er10_tp.png){#fig-res4-tp}

![Wind speed exposure-response relationship (Lag 0), disaggregated by population groups](figures/MF_4_disag_er0_fg10.png){#fig-res4-fg10}

## Analysis 5: Emergency ward results

Taking a step back, we initially set out to examine the effects of weather on emergency admissions. Most sites have incomplete time series data collected by their respective emergency departments, this was not possible. However, we can conduct a case study and analyze a single site that does have a complete times series: Hamirpur.

Though slightly diffeent, the overall distributions (@fig-res5-overall) do not vary much from the total patient distributions observed in the pooled effects models (Analysis 1). When examining the exposure response distributions by lags (@fig-res5-er), precipitation and wind speed have no effect. Temperature distributions are similar to total patient admission patterns, though admission increase by over 10% when temperatures dip below the 20th percentile, 14 days after exposure.

This is only a single site so cannot be generalised, but these outputs suggest a minimal different between total patient and emergency ward trends.

![Cummulative relative risk (RR) of exposure-response for total hospital admissions across all time for each weather predictors. Temperature and precipitation use the 50th and 0th percentile as reference, respectively.](figures/MF_5A_emg_overall.png){#fig-res5-overall}

# Summary

Overall, our models are very sensitive to parameter selection. I think we are a point where these are shifting less but it is clear that, for this context, weather has a small and even negligible effect on hospital admissions (partners warned us of this from the onset). It is possible that autocorrelation is obscuring these outputs, but without a clear way forward to account for this, this is where our outputs stand.

Moving forward, I am going to discuss these outputs with parters to get a sense of how reliable the model is capturing the city specific patterns. I am also trying to arrange a meeting with Antonio Gasparrini to discuss the parameters selection process and see if he can shed more light on this. Once I have sense checked the method and outputs, we can move ahead with this.
